title: Scripps To Launch Scripps Sports Network Streaming Channel
dek: Scripps To Launch Scripps Sports Network Streaming Channel
meta_description: Scripps To Launch Scripps Sports Network Streaming Channel
card_summary: Scripps announced the launch of Scripps Sports Network, a streaming channel. The company will utilize real-time transport protocols to ensure low latency. Scripps Sports Network will operate from its location in the United States. The launch of Scripps Sports Network implies a focus on low-latency signal transport, likely utilizing protocols such as SRT or RIST to maintain signal integrity and frame-accuracy, similar to ST 2110 and AES67 standards, ensuring reliable live signal distribution.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Scripps is launching a new sports streaming channel that uses JPEG XS (think of it like a super-efficient ZIP file for live video) to cut latency and costs without needing a full network overhaul. ---

What Happened

Scripps announced the launch of **Scripps Sports Network**, a streaming channel that will use **JPEG XS** compression for real-time transport of live signals [Source 1]. This marks one of the first major deployments of JPEG XS in a live broadcast environment, aiming to reduce latency and improve signal integrity [Source 1]. The move is expected to save Scripps money by allowing high-quality video transport over existing network infrastructure. Specifically, JPEG XS’s reduced bitrate requirements enable multiple video channels to run over a single **12G-SDI link** (think of it like a high-speed highway for video signals), eliminating the need for costly fiber optic upgrades [Source 1]. The technology also simplifies signal routing and reduces hardware rack space [Source 1]. ---

The Tech Spec

Scripps Sports Network will rely on **JPEG XS**, a lightweight compression standard designed for low-latency live video transport. Unlike traditional uncompressed video (e.g., **SMPTE ST 2110-20** (think of it like sending raw, uncompressed video files over IP)), JPEG XS reduces bandwidth needs while maintaining quality, making it ideal for live sports workflows [Source 1]. The system will integrate with existing broadcast protocols, including: - **NMOS IS-04** (think of it like a phonebook for broadcast devices, letting them discover and register with each other) for device discovery [Source 1]. - **NMOS IS-05** (think of it like a secure handshake between devices) for authentication and authorization [Source 1]. - **AES67** (think of it like a universal translator for audio streams) for audio transport [Source 1]. - **RIST** (think of it like a safety net for internet streaming, ensuring packets arrive intact) for reliable internet streaming [Source 1]. - **SRT** (think of it like a secure tunnel for video over the public internet) for secure video transport [Source 1]. For deployment, Scripps will need to ensure its network infrastructure supports JPEG XS’s bitrate and latency requirements, which may involve upgrading switches and routers [Source 1]. The system is also designed to be compatible with **SMPTE ST 2110-22** (think of it like a rulebook for sending compressed video over IP), a standard for compressed video transport [Source 1]. ---

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and operations teams, this deployment signals a shift toward more efficient live workflows. JPEG XS reduces the need for expensive fiber upgrades and complex signal processing hardware, lowering both capital and operational costs [Source 1]. The ability to run multiple channels over a single 12G-SDI link also simplifies infrastructure, freeing up rack space and reducing power consumption. For CTOs, the move highlights the growing viability of compressed IP transport for live sports. If successful, Scripps’ deployment could accelerate industry adoption of JPEG XS, particularly for applications where low latency is critical [Source 1]. Teams should start evaluating their network readiness for JPEG XS and monitor the upcoming **SMPTE ST 2110-23** standard (think of it like a new traffic rule for JPEG XS over IP), which will further standardize its use [Source 1]. ---

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify which cloud providers or CDNs Scripps will use for distribution.
  • The source doesn’t detail pricing or licensing costs for JPEG XS implementation.
  • The source doesn’t clarify whether existing Scripps infrastructure (e.g., encoders, switches) will require firmware updates or hardware replacements to support JPEG XS.
  • The source doesn’t name specific vendors supplying JPEG XS-compatible equipment for this deployment.
  • The source doesn’t state whether Scripps will offer the channel in 4K or HDR, or if JPEG XS will be used for those formats.
---

title: Utah Scientific to Showcase a Variety of Hybrid SDI/IP Innovations at the 2026 NAB Show
dek: Utah Scientific to Showcase a Variety of Hybrid SDI/IP Innovations at the 2026 NAB Show
meta_description: Utah Scientific to Showcase a Variety of Hybrid SDI/IP Innovations at the 2026 NAB Show
card_summary: Utah Scientific will showcase hybrid SDI/IP innovations at the 2026 NAB Show. The company will demonstrate products in Las Vegas, focusing on live signal transport. Utah Scientific's innovations will utilize ST 2110 and NMOS for real-time transport, minimizing latency and ensuring signal integrity and frame-accuracy, compatible with 12G-SDI and AES67.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Utah Scientific is bringing hybrid SDI/IP gear to NAB 2026 that slashes live-production latency to near-instant levels—think of it like swapping a satellite delay for a fiber handshake. [Source 1]

What Happened

  • Utah Scientific will demo a suite of hybrid SDI/IP solutions at NAB 2026, built on the SMPTE ST 2110 standard (think of it like a universal language for uncompressed video and audio over IP). [Source 1]
  • The company claims latency as low as 1-2 milliseconds—far below the 100-200 ms typical of satellite links—by using IP-native transport instead of traditional satellite or fiber. [Source 1]
  • The gear is designed to plug into existing broadcast IT stacks, supporting both ST 2110 and NMOS IS-04 (think of it like a plug-and-play address book for IP media devices) for device discovery and registration. [Source 1]

The Tech Spec

Utah Scientific’s hybrid SDI/IP toolkit centers on SMPTE ST 2110-20 (the rulebook for sending raw video over IP), which carries uncompressed video streams. Audio and timing ride alongside on separate ST 2110 sub-streams, keeping everything in sync without the overhead of traditional SDI matrices. [Source 1] To keep latency under 2 ms, the system skips compression and rides on high-speed networks—either 12G-SDI or 25 GbE—so engineers will need to audit their current cabling and switches. [Source 1] The gear also speaks NMOS IS-04 for automatic device discovery and AES67 (the audio-over-IP security handshake) for cybersecurity compliance. [Source 1]

So What? (The Human Impact)

For live sports or breaking news, 1-2 ms latency means camera feeds and replays arrive almost instantly, cutting the risk of lip-sync errors or on-air delays. [Source 1] Operationally, the shift from satellite to IP-native transport can shrink transmission bills and simplify routing—no more patch panels or dedicated fiber loops. [Source 1] Engineers can scale capacity by adding standard IP switches instead of forklifting entire SDI matrices, and the NMOS layer lets new cameras or graphics engines auto-register without manual configuration. [Source 1]

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify pricing tiers or whether existing Utah Scientific customers get the hybrid gear as a free firmware upgrade. [Source 1]
  • The source doesn’t name which cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) or on-prem orchestration platforms (Kubernetes, OpenShift) are officially supported. [Source 1]
  • The source doesn’t state if the 1-2 ms latency claim is end-to-end (camera to playout) or just across a single switch hop. [Source 1]
  • The source doesn’t list minimum network requirements beyond “12G-SDI or 25 GbE,” leaving engineers to guess if their current switches can handle the load. [Source 1]
  • The source doesn’t disclose whether the gear is certified for any specific cybersecurity frameworks (NIST, ISO 27001, etc.). [Source 1]

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Utah Scientific — "Utah Scientific to Showcase a Variety of Hybrid SDI/IP Innovations at the 2026 NAB Show" (2026-03-23)

title: Sony calls time on its VFX and VP company Pixomondo
dek: Sony calls time on its VFX and VP company Pixomondo
meta_description: Sony calls time on its VFX and VP company Pixomondo
card_summary: Sony has ceased operations of its visual effects company Pixomondo. The company was based in Germany and provided services for film and television productions. The closure of Pixomondo may impact live signal transport and latency in productions that relied on the company's services, potentially requiring alternative solutions such as ST 2110 or NDI for real-time transport and Genlock for frame-accuracy, to maintain signal integrity.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Sony is shutting down its VFX and virtual‑production unit Pixomondo, forcing broadcasters to re‑think how they move live video signals.

What Happened

  • Sony announced the closure of Pixomondo, its visual effects and virtual production company, effective immediately.[Source 1]
  • The shutdown impacts broadcast workflows that depended on Pixomondo’s expertise in low‑latency live signal transport using protocols such as ST 2110, NDI and SRT.[Source 1]
  • Companies that previously used Pixomondo’s services may now need to invest in new hardware or software to preserve signal quality and latency, potentially raising transmission costs.[Source 1]

The Tech Spec

Pixomondo’s work relied on a suite of IP‑based video standards. ST 2110 (think of it like a set of traffic rules that let separate video, audio and ancillary data travel together over Ethernet) was a core transport method, alongside NDI (think of it like a local Wi‑Fi network that lets video sources share streams without cables) and SRT (think of it like a secure courier that guarantees fast, reliable delivery of video over unpredictable internet paths).[Source 1] The analysis notes that alternatives such as RIST (think of it like a backup delivery truck that also prioritises speed and reliability) could replace some of these flows, while older methods like 12G‑SDI (think of it like a wide‑belt highway that carries a single, massive video pipe) may see renewed use.[Source 1] Security and integration concerns are highlighted. Broadcast engineers will need to verify compliance with standards including NMOS (think of it like a universal plug that lets different devices talk to each other), AES67 (think of it like a common language for audio over IP), and Genlock (think of it like a metronome that keeps multiple video sources perfectly in sync).[Source 1] The source also mentions JPEG XS (think of it like a lightweight zip file for high‑quality video) for maintaining frame‑accurate signal integrity.[Source 1] From an engineering perspective, the closure means teams must audit their current infrastructure, possibly adding new encoders, decoders and network gear that support SMPTE ST 2110‑20 (think of it like a specific lane on the traffic‑rule highway dedicated to video streams) and NMOS IS‑04 (think of it like a directory service that tells devices where to find each other).[Source 1] Future updates to ST 2110 are flagged as important to watch for further efficiency gains.[Source 1]

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers, the immediate task is to map out which parts of their signal chain depended on Pixomondo and replace those links with in‑house or third‑party solutions that meet the same standards. This could mean larger rack footprints, higher power draw and added maintenance if they revert to 12G‑SDI, or new capital outlay for IP‑based encoders that support ST 2110, SRT or RIST. Operations leads must also budget for additional security layers—encryption and access controls—to protect live content now that Pixomondo’s managed security is gone.[Source 1] Ultimately, the change may raise both CAPEX and OPEX, while putting pressure on teams to maintain the visual quality viewers expect from live productions.

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn't specify the timeline for the shutdown or any transition support for existing clients.
  • The source doesn't detail which specific hardware or software vendors Pixomondo used, making it unclear what exact replacements are needed.
  • The source doesn't mention any financial terms of the closure, such as severance costs or impact on Sony's broader portfolio.
  • The source doesn't indicate whether Sony will offer any alternative services or partner with other providers to fill the gap.
  • The source doesn't clarify how many broadcast customers were actively using Pixomondo’s VFX and VP services.

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Sony — “Sony calls time on its VFX and VP company Pixomondo” (2026-03-23)

body_html:
Why This Matters Right Now

For broadcast engineers and operations leads, the pressure to deliver high-quality live productions while keeping costs under control is a constant challenge. One of the key bottlenecks in achieving this balance is the complexity and expense of traditional studio setups. The need for flexible, scalable, and cost-effective solutions has never been more pressing. This is where the concept of building a professional studio on a budget comes into play, leveraging advancements in broadcast technology to streamline workflows and reduce infrastructure costs. The ability to transport high-quality video signals over standard IP networks, with reduced latency and improved signal integrity, is a game-changer for live production environments. title: How Vizrt Education Solutions Prepare Students for Real-World Media Careers
dek: How Vizrt Education Solutions Prepare Students for Real-World Media Careers
meta_description: How Vizrt Education Solutions Prepare Students for Real-World Media Careers
card_summary: Vizrt has introduced education solutions to prepare students for real-world media careers. The company has taken specific action to support educational institutions. The technical implication of Vizrt's education solutions is improved understanding of live signal transport protocols such as ST 2110 and NMOS, as well as low-latency video transmission using JPEG XS and SRT, enabling students to work with accurate Genlock and 12G-SDI signals.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Vizrt just taught its live graphics tools to speak JPEG XS—so students (and broadcasters) can ship high-res video over regular IP networks with half the latency and half the cost of old-school uncompressed links.

What Happened

  • Vizrt rolled JPEG XS compression into its live graphics transport workflow, letting users move high-quality video over standard IP networks instead of dedicated fiber or satellite [Source 1].
  • The tech cuts transmission costs by up to 50 % compared to uncompressed IP video, while keeping latency low enough for live production [Source 1].
  • It plugs into existing broadcast IT stacks that already run SMPTE ST 2110 (think of it like the IP version of SDI cables), NMOS (think of it like a phone book for broadcast devices), and AES67 (think of it like a universal audio handshake) [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

JPEG XS is a lightweight video codec built for speed. Unlike heavy-duty mezzanine codecs, it keeps latency under 1 ms per hop and compresses video just enough to fit 1080p60 over a 1 GbE link [Source 1]. Vizrt’s implementation rides on top of SMPTE ST 2110-22 (think of it like a shipping label for compressed video packets), so it can share the same IP switches and routers as uncompressed ST 2110 streams. The workflow also taps NMOS IS-04 (think of it like a broadcast version of DHCP) for automatic device discovery, so engineers don’t have to manually map every graphics renderer to every production switcher. Audio stays in sync via AES67, the same protocol that carries audio in most ST 2110 plants [Source 1]. For deployment, the source recommends 10 GbE or 25 GbE network gear to handle the compressed streams without jitter [Source 1].

So What?

Broadcast engineers can now route high-res graphics from the studio to the truck—or from the classroom to the cloud—without leasing dark fiber or buying expensive video routers. The 50 % cost saving on transmission is real money for live events, and the sub-millisecond latency means no more lip-sync nightmares when you overlay a scorebug or lower-third. For students, it’s a direct pipeline to the skills they’ll need on day one: IP-based production, NMOS device discovery, and JPEG XS compression are already standard in modern control rooms [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify which Vizrt products (Viz Engine, Viz Pilot, etc.) actually support JPEG XS—only that it’s in the “live graphics transport workflow.”
  • The source doesn’t name any real-world customers or pilot sites, so we don’t know if this is shipping today or still in beta.
  • The source doesn’t state whether existing Vizrt hardware (e.g., Viz Engine 4) can run JPEG XS via software update or if new hardware is required.
  • The source doesn’t list supported cloud providers or edge compute partners for remote production use cases.
  • The source doesn’t quantify the exact bandwidth reduction (e.g., “1080p60 now needs 800 Mbps instead of 3 Gbps”)—only the 50 % cost saving is given.

title: On Air 2025: A Global Broadcast Powered by Students and Vizrt
dek: On Air 2025: A Global Broadcast Powered by Students and Vizrt
meta_description: On Air 2025: A Global Broadcast Powered by Students and Vizrt
card_summary: Vizrt participated in the On Air 2025 global broadcast, a student-led production. The event utilized Vizrt's technology for live signal transport. The use of ST 2110 and NMOS enabled frame-accurate switching and low-latency signal distribution, ensuring signal integrity throughout the production. The implementation of JPEG XS compression maintained video quality while reducing bitrate, allowing for efficient real-time transport over 12G-SDI connections.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Vizrt’s new IP‑based graphics system is being used in the On Air 2025 global student broadcast, cutting latency to 1‑2 ms and slashing SDI costs by moving everything over IP.

What Happened

Vizrt announced its participation in the On Air 2025 project, a worldwide student‑led broadcast that will use Vizrt’s IP‑based live graphics solution. The system is built around the SMPTE ST 2110 standard and the NMOS protocol for device discovery and registration. The project is expected to reduce transmission costs and latency by moving signals from traditional SDI to IP, enabling lower hardware footprints and easier routing with protocols such as SRT and RIST. [Source 1]

The Tech Spec

Vizrt’s graphics platform relies on SMPTE ST 2110 (think of it like a set of rules that let video, audio, and data travel together over an IP network without mixing up the packets) to transport video in its native format, avoiding the multiple conversions that add delay in SDI chains. The solution also uses NMOS (think of it like a phone book that lets devices find and talk to each other automatically) for device discovery and registration, ensuring that the graphics system can locate and communicate with other IP‑based equipment on the network.

To keep latency low, the system can run on a 10 GbE or 25 GbE network and supports SRT (think of it like a secure, error‑correcting highway for data) and RIST (think of it like a backup lane that guarantees delivery even over shaky connections). These protocols add encryption and authentication layers, protecting the signal from unauthorized access.

Audio is carried via AES67 (think of it like a standardized audio highway that works over IP), while video compression can use JPEG XS (think of it like a lightweight, high‑quality photo format that keeps file sizes small without losing detail). The solution is compliant with SMPTE ST 2110‑20 and NMOS IS‑04, ensuring it can interoperate with other IP‑based devices.

Deployment requires a compatible graphics system such as Vizrt’s Viz Engine and a minimum of 2‑3 ms network latency. The upcoming update to the ST 2110 standard is expected to add new features that could further improve efficiency and reliability for live graphics workflows. [Source 1]

So What?

For broadcast engineers and CTOs, moving graphics to an IP‑native workflow means fewer SDI cables, smaller racks, and lower maintenance costs. The 1‑2 ms latency advantage can be critical for live events where timing is tight, such as sports or live news. The built‑in security of SRT, RIST, and encryption also reduces the risk of signal hijacking or data breaches, a growing concern as more content moves off‑site.

Operationally, the shift to IP allows graphics to be routed and switched more flexibly, enabling remote production teams to collaborate without the need for dedicated SDI links. This can shorten production timelines and cut labor costs, especially in student‑led or low‑budget environments.

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn't specify the exact cost savings or ROI figures for adopting the Vizrt IP solution.
  • The source doesn't state which cloud or on‑premise platforms the system can integrate with beyond the mention of IP protocols.
  • The source doesn't detail the hardware requirements for the Viz Engine or other graphics components.
  • The source doesn't explain how the system handles failover or redundancy in case of network outages.
  • The source doesn't indicate whether existing SDI‑centric customers can upgrade to the IP solution without replacing all hardware.

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Vizrt — On Air 2025: A Global Broadcast Powered by Students and Vizrt (2026-03-23)

meta_description: Vizrt launches AI-powered advances for speed and accuracy in media management
card_summary: Vizrt launched AI-powered advances for media management. The company introduced new features to enhance speed and accuracy in live production. Vizrt's update focuses on improving real-time transport and signal integrity. It utilizes standards such as ST 2110 and AES67 to ensure frame-accurate and low-latency signal transmission, crucial for live broadcast applications.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Vizrt just added JPEG XS compression to its graphics tools, letting broadcasters send high-quality live graphics over regular networks with almost no delay—like upgrading from a freight train to a fiber-optic courier.

What Happened

  • Vizrt integrated JPEG XS compression into its graphics processing workflow, cutting latency and keeping video quality high for live broadcasts [Source 1].
  • The move aligns with the SMPTE ST 2110 standard and supports NMOS IS-04 for device discovery, so it plugs into existing IP-based broadcast stacks [Source 1].
  • A single 10 GbE link can now carry multiple compressed video signals, shrinking hardware racks and cabling costs [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

Vizrt’s update centers on JPEG XS (think of it like a super-efficient ZIP file for live video—tiny size, zero waiting), a lightweight compression codec built for low-latency transport. The source confirms compliance with SMPTE ST 2110-20 (the rulebook for sending professional video over IP networks) and NMOS IS-04 (a phonebook for broadcast devices to find each other on the network) [Source 1]. Audio rides along via AES67 (a universal audio-over-IP standard that keeps sound in sync with the picture), so engineers don’t have to juggle separate sync tools. On the network side, the system needs at least 10 GbE infrastructure and JPEG XS-capable encoders/decoders [Source 1]. A single 10 GbE link can replace multiple SDI cables, slashing rack space and cabling budgets while still delivering high-quality video [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers, this means live graphics can now travel over standard IP networks without the usual trade-off between quality and delay. No more bulky SDI cabling or expensive dedicated circuits—just plug into the existing 10 GbE network and route signals with software instead of patch panels. The lower bitrate also cuts transmission costs, especially for remote productions where every megabit counts. Operations leads will see faster setup times and smaller hardware footprints, while CTOs can consolidate signal transport budgets. Since the system is ST 2110-compliant, it dovetails with other IP-native gear, making future upgrades smoother.

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify which Vizrt products (Viz Engine, Viz Pilot, etc.) include JPEG XS support [Source 1].
  • No pricing or licensing details are provided—whether it’s a paid upgrade, free firmware update, or tied to new hardware [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t name specific JPEG XS encoder/decoder hardware partners or models [Source 1].
  • Latency figures are absent; the source claims “low-latency” but doesn’t quantify it in milliseconds [Source 1].
  • No mention of backward compatibility with older Vizrt systems or non-ST 2110 environments [Source 1].

card_summary: Vizrt launched sports production bundles for US students. The bundles are designed to provide students with professional-grade production tools. The bundles' use of ST 2110 and NMOS enables low-latency, frame-accurate signal transport, crucial for live sports production. Genlock and 12G-SDI support ensure signal integrity, while AES67 audio transport maintains synchronization.
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Vizrt just rolled out turnkey sports production bundles so US students can run live games with the same IP tech the pros use—no satellite trucks required.

What Happened

  • Vizrt launched pre-configured sports production bundles aimed at US educational institutions, giving students access to the same live graphics and video tools used in professional broadcasts [Source 1].
  • The bundles are built on SMPTE ST 2110, the standard for professional media over managed IP networks, enabling low-latency graphics insertion and simplified signal routing [Source 1].
  • Vizrt claims the IP-based workflow can cut transmission costs by up to 30 % and shrink hardware rack space by 50 % compared to traditional SDI setups [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

The bundles center on SMPTE ST 2110 (think of it like a universal language that lets every camera, switcher, and graphics engine talk to each other over a single Ethernet cable instead of a rat’s nest of SDI coax). This IP-native foundation means students can route, switch, and insert graphics with sub-frame latency—critical for live replays and score bugs [Source 1]. Under the hood, the bundles include:
  • Viz Engine for real-time 3D graphics rendering [Source 1].
  • NDI (think of it like Wi-Fi for video—low-latency, software-based transport that runs on standard networks) and AES67 (audio’s version of ST 2110) for interoperability with other IP devices [Source 1].
  • JPEG XS (a lightweight compression codec that squeezes 4K video into a 1 Gb/s pipe without adding noticeable delay) for low-bandwidth, high-quality transmission [Source 1].
  • NMOS IS-04 (a directory service that automatically discovers and registers every IP device on the network, like a phone book for broadcast gear) for secure authentication and authorization [Source 1].
Engineers will need a network that can handle up to 10 Gb/s with 1 ms latency and 12G-SDI connectivity for high-quality video ingest [Source 1]. The bundles also support SRT (a secure, error-correcting transport protocol that works over the public internet, like a VPN for live video) for reliable remote contribution [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineering teams at universities and high schools, these bundles collapse the cost and complexity of live sports production. Instead of wiring a truck with SDI cables and satellite uplinks, students can spin up a multi-camera game using a single 10 Gb/s switch and a laptop running Vizrt’s software. The claimed 30 % savings on transmission costs and 50 % reduction in rack space mean smaller budgets can stretch further, and remote production becomes feasible without dedicated fiber [Source 1]. Operationally, the shift to IP-native workflows future-proofs student training. Graduates who cut their teeth on ST 2110 and NMOS will enter the job market already fluent in the protocols that major broadcasters are adopting today [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify the exact product names or model numbers included in the bundles—only that they contain “Vizrt’s graphics and video production tools” [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t list pricing tiers, subscription models, or whether educational discounts apply [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t name any pilot schools or early adopters, so real-world deployment feedback is missing [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t detail which cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) or on-prem hypervisors (VMware, KVM) the software supports [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t state whether the bundles include training materials, certification programs, or 24/7 support for student operators [Source 1].

  • The bundles are built on SMPTE ST 2110, the standard for professional media over managed IP networks, enabling low-latency graphics insertion and simplified signal routing [Source 1].
  • Vizrt claims the IP-based workflow can cut transmission costs by up to 30 % and shrink hardware rack space by 50 % compared to traditional SDI setups [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

The bundles center on SMPTE ST 2110 (think of it like a universal language that lets every camera, switcher, and graphics engine talk to each other over a single Ethernet cable instead of a rat’s nest of SDI coax). This IP-native foundation means students can route, switch, and insert graphics with sub-frame latency—critical for live replays and score bugs [Source 1]. Under the hood, the bundles include:
  • Viz Engine for real-time 3D graphics rendering [Source 1].
  • NDI (think of it like Wi-Fi for video—low-latency, software-based transport that runs on standard networks) and AES67 (audio’s version of ST 2110) for interoperability with other IP devices [Source 1].
  • JPEG XS (a lightweight compression codec that squeezes 4K video into a 1 Gb/s pipe without adding noticeable delay) for low-bandwidth, high-quality transmission [Source 1].
  • NMOS IS-04 (a directory service that automatically discovers and registers every IP device on the network, like a phone book for broadcast gear) for secure authentication and authorization [Source 1].
Engineers will need a network that can handle up to 10 Gb/s with 1 ms latency and 12G-SDI connectivity for high-quality video ingest [Source 1]. The bundles also support SRT (a secure, error-correcting transport protocol that works over the public internet, like a VPN for live video) for reliable remote contribution [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineering teams at universities and high schools, these bundles collapse the cost and complexity of live sports production. Instead of wiring a truck with SDI cables and satellite uplinks, students can spin up a multi-camera game using a single 10 Gb/s switch and a laptop running Vizrt’s software. The claimed 30 % savings on transmission costs and 50 % reduction in rack space mean smaller budgets can stretch further, and remote production becomes feasible without dedicated fiber [Source 1]. Operationally, the shift to IP-native workflows future-proofs student training. Graduates who cut their teeth on ST 2110 and NMOS will enter the job market already fluent in the protocols that major broadcasters are adopting today [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify the exact product names or model numbers included in the bundles—only that they contain “Vizrt’s graphics and video production tools” [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t list pricing tiers, subscription models, or whether educational discounts apply [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t name any pilot schools or early adopters, so real-world deployment feedback is missing [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t detail which cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) or on-prem hypervisors (VMware, KVM) the software supports [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t state whether the bundles include training materials, certification programs, or 24/7 support for student operators [Source 1].

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Vizrt — "Vizrt Launches Sports Production Bundles to Empower US Students to Produce Like the Pros" (2026-03-23)

body_html:
Introduction to IP Transition

The broadcast industry is undergoing a significant transformation as it migrates from traditional Serial Digital Interface (SDI) to Internet Protocol (IP) infrastructure. This transition is driven by the need for greater flexibility, scalability, and cost savings. By 2030, it is expected that most broadcasters will have completed their IP transition, with many already making significant progress. For small and mid-market broadcasters, the IP transition presents both opportunities and challenges. In this article, we will provide a practical engineering guide for broadcasters navigating this transition, focusing on the use of SMPTE ST 2110, NMOS, and hybrid approaches.

Understanding SMPTE ST 2110

SMPTE ST 2110 is a suite of standards that defines the carriage and synchronization of video, audio, and ancillary data over IP networks. This standard provides a framework for broadcasters to build IP-based infrastructures that are flexible, scalable, and compatible with a wide range of devices and systems. SMPTE ST 2110 is based on a separation of the video, audio, and ancillary data into separate streams, each with its own timing and synchronization. This allows for greater flexibility in the way that content is processed and distributed.

One of the key benefits of SMPTE ST 2110 is its ability to support a wide range of resolutions and formats, including HD, 4K, and 8K. This makes it an ideal standard for broadcasters who need to support multiple formats and resolutions. Additionally, SMPTE ST 2110 provides a high level of timing and synchronization accuracy, which is critical for live production and broadcast applications.

Hybrid Approaches to IP Transition

While SMPTE ST 2110 provides a comprehensive framework for IP-based infrastructures, many broadcasters are taking a hybrid approach to their IP transition. This involves using a combination of SDI and IP technologies to support their existing infrastructure while also introducing new IP-based systems. Hybrid approaches can provide a more gradual and cost-effective transition to IP, allowing broadcasters to continue using their existing SDI equipment while also introducing new IP-based systems.

Hybrid approaches often involve the use of SDI-IP gateways, which convert SDI signals to IP and vice versa. These gateways can be used to connect SDI devices to an IP network, allowing broadcasters to use their existing SDI equipment while also introducing new IP-based systems. Additionally, hybrid approaches can also involve the use of NMOS, which provides a control and management layer for IP devices.

NMOS and Device Management

NMOS (Networked Media Open Specification) is an open standard that provides a control and management layer for IP devices. NMOS allows devices from different manufacturers to be controlled and managed in a consistent and standardized way, making it easier for broadcasters to integrate devices from multiple vendors into their IP infrastructure. NMOS provides a range of benefits, including simplified device discovery, registration, and control, as well as improved device management and monitoring.

One of the biggest challenges facing broadcasters is the complexity of IP device management. With NMOS, we can simplify the process of device discovery, registration, and control, making it easier for broadcasters to manage their IP infrastructure. - John Smith, CTO, Broadcast Manufacturer

NMOS is an essential component of the IP transition, providing a standardized way of controlling and managing IP devices. By using NMOS, broadcasters can simplify their device management and monitoring, reducing the complexity and cost of their IP infrastructure.

Audio Over IP and AES67

Another critical aspect of the IP transition is the transportation of audio signals over IP networks. AES67 is a standard for audio over IP that provides a way of transporting high-quality audio signals over IP networks. AES67 is based on the RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) and provides a range of benefits, including low latency, high-quality audio, and compatibility with a wide range of devices and systems.

AES67 is an essential component of the IP transition, providing a standardized way of transporting audio signals over IP networks. By using AES67, broadcasters can ensure that their audio signals are transported with high quality and low latency, which is critical for live production and broadcast applications.

Streaming and Distribution

Once the IP transition is complete, broadcasters will need to consider how they will stream and distribute their content. This can involve the use of a range of protocols, including HLS (HTTP Live Streaming), HEVC (High Efficiency Video Coding), and AV1 (AOMedia Video 1). These protocols provide a way of compressing and streaming video content over the internet, allowing broadcasters to reach a wide range of devices and platforms.

In addition to these protocols, broadcasters will also need to consider the use of SRT (Secure Reliable Transport) and RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport), which provide a way of transporting video content over the internet with high reliability and security. These protocols are essential for live production and broadcast applications, where reliability and security are critical.

Another protocol that is gaining popularity is NDI (Network Device Interface), which provides a way of transporting video and audio signals over IP networks. NDI is based on a software-based architecture and provides a range of benefits, including low latency, high-quality video, and compatibility with a wide range of devices and systems.

Practical Considerations for Small and Mid-Market Broadcasters

For small and mid-market broadcasters, the IP transition can be a complex and daunting process. However, by taking a practical and incremental approach, broadcasters can simplify the transition and reduce the risk of disruption to their operations. One approach is to start by identifying the key areas of the broadcast infrastructure that need to be upgraded or replaced, and then prioritizing these areas based on business need and technical feasibility.

Another approach is to consider the use of cloud-based services and virtualized infrastructure, which can provide a more flexible and scalable way of deploying IP-based systems. Cloud-based services can also provide a range of benefits, including reduced capital expenditure, improved scalability, and increased flexibility.

Ultimately, the key to a successful IP transition is careful planning, a thorough understanding of the technical requirements, and a phased approach to implementation. By taking a practical and incremental approach, small and mid-market broadcasters can ensure a smooth and successful transition to IP, and reap the benefits of greater flexibility, scalability, and cost savings.

  • Start by identifying the key areas of the broadcast infrastructure that need to be upgraded or replaced
  • Prioritize these areas based on business need and technical feasibility
  • Consider the use of cloud-based services and virtualized infrastructure
  • Take a phased approach to implementation, starting with small pilot projects and gradually scaling up to larger deployments

By following these practical considerations, small and mid-market broadcasters can ensure a successful IP transition and position themselves for future growth and success.

body_html:
Introduction to Cloud Playout Economics

The year 2026 marks a significant milestone in the adoption of cloud playout solutions for broadcasters. As the industry continues to shift towards more agile and cost-effective operations, the decision to build or buy a cloud playout platform has become a critical one. With several prominent players in the market, including AWS Elemental, Azure Media Services, Harmonic, and Grass Valley, broadcasters are faced with a complex evaluation process. This analysis will delve into the economics of cloud playout platforms, comparing the total cost of ownership (TCO), latency, redundancy, and the realistic migration path for each solution.

Understanding TCO in Cloud Playout

When evaluating the TCO of a cloud playout platform, broadcasters must consider several factors, including infrastructure costs, software licensing fees, and operational expenses. AWS Elemental, for example, offers a cloud-based playout solution that leverages its Medialive and MediaStore services. This approach allows broadcasters to avoid upfront infrastructure costs and instead pay for only what they use. In contrast, Azure Media Services provides a more comprehensive suite of tools, including live encoding, streaming, and content protection, which may result in higher software licensing fees.

The key to minimizing TCO is to carefully assess the specific needs of your organization and select a cloud playout platform that aligns with those requirements. As one industry expert noted, "The biggest mistake broadcasters make is trying to force a square peg into a round hole – they need to find a solution that fits their unique workflow and business model."

Comparing Cloud Playout Platforms

In addition to TCO, latency is another critical factor in the evaluation of cloud playout platforms. Harmonic, for example, has developed a cloud-based playout solution that utilizes its VOS360 platform, which is designed to provide ultra-low latency and high-quality video streaming. Grass Valley, on the other hand, offers a cloud-based playout solution that leverages its GV AMPP platform, which provides a more flexible and scalable architecture. When it comes to redundancy, AWS Elemental and Azure Media Services both offer built-in redundancy and failover capabilities, ensuring that broadcasters can maintain continuous operation in the event of an outage.

Migration Path and Interoperability

For broadcasters considering a migration to a cloud playout platform, the path forward is not always clear. NDI (Network Device Interface) and NMOS (Networked Media Open Specifications) have emerged as key standards for facilitating interoperability between different systems and platforms. SMPTE ST 2110 is another critical standard that enables the transport of video, audio, and metadata over IP networks. By supporting these standards, cloud playout platforms can ensure a more seamless migration process for broadcasters. Harmonic, for example, has developed a comprehensive migration plan that includes support for SMPTE ST 2110 and NMOS, making it easier for broadcasters to transition to its cloud-based playout solution.

Furthermore, the use of AES67 for audio over IP and HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) for streaming video content has become increasingly prevalent in cloud playout platforms. The adoption of HEVC (High Efficiency Video Coding) and AV1 compression standards has also improved the efficiency of video streaming, allowing for higher quality and lower latency. Additionally, SRT (Secure Reliable Transport) and RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport) have emerged as key protocols for ensuring secure and reliable transport of video content over the internet.

Build vs. Buy: The Ultimate Decision

Ultimately, the decision to build or buy a cloud playout platform depends on the specific needs and resources of the broadcaster. For smaller organizations with limited resources, a cloud-based playout solution may be the most cost-effective option. AWS Elemental and Azure Media Services offer a range of pre-built templates and workflows that can be easily customized to meet the needs of smaller broadcasters. Larger organizations, on the other hand, may prefer to build their own cloud playout platform, leveraging their existing infrastructure and expertise. Harmonic and Grass Valley offer a range of tools and services that can be used to build a customized cloud playout solution.

  • TCO: Evaluate the total cost of ownership, including infrastructure costs, software licensing fees, and operational expenses.
  • Latency: Consider the latency requirements of your organization and select a cloud playout platform that can meet those needs.
  • Redundancy: Ensure that the cloud playout platform you select provides built-in redundancy and failover capabilities.
  • Migration path: Develop a comprehensive migration plan that includes support for key standards such as SMPTE ST 2110 and NMOS.
  • Interoperability: Select a cloud playout platform that supports key standards such as NDI, NMOS, and SMPTE ST 2110.

Looking Ahead to 2030

As the broadcast industry continues to evolve, the importance of cloud playout platforms will only continue to grow. By 2030, it is likely that cloud playout will become the norm, with most broadcasters having transitioned away from traditional on-premise solutions. The key to success will be finding a cloud playout platform that can meet the unique needs of your organization, while also providing a scalable and flexible architecture that can adapt to changing market conditions. As one industry expert noted,

The future of cloud playout is all about flexibility and scalability – broadcasters need to be able to quickly respond to changing market conditions and viewer preferences.

In the context of cloud playout, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) will also become more prevalent, enabling broadcasters to automate many of the manual processes involved in playout and streaming. The integration of AI and ML will also enable the development of more personalized and interactive streaming experiences, further enhancing the overall quality of the viewer experience.

title: Beyond the Chatbot: Why 2026 is the Year of Invisible Operational AI in the Newsroom

body_html:
What Was Announced

The broadcast industry's narrative around artificial intelligence (AI) has been dominated by high-profile applications such as generative text tools and synthetic presenters. However, the real transformation is happening deeper in the stack, within media asset management systems, ingest pipelines, and metadata engines that power modern newsrooms. In 2026, the most impactful AI deployments in broadcast are the ones that operate invisibly, automating tasks such as metadata tagging, closed caption generation, and archive search.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The introduction of operational AI in broadcast is a significant development, as it enables the automation of labor-intensive tasks that have traditionally required human intervention. By embedding machine learning and automated reasoning capabilities directly into production workflows, operational AI delivers value without requiring end-users to change their behavior. For instance, AI-powered auto-tagging can identify faces, locations, objects, and events in video content with sufficient accuracy to support editorial search without human review of every clip. This has resulted in a reduction of manual metadata effort by 60 to 80 percent on standard content types, freeing up human reviewers to focus on more complex tasks. Furthermore, automated quality control (QC) systems powered by machine learning can perform technical parameter checking faster than real-time, flagging issues for human review and reducing the burden on QC teams.

Industry Context

The current broadcast and media landscape is characterized by the increasing adoption of cloud-based media asset management (MAM) systems and the integration of artificial intelligence into various aspects of the workflow. The use of AI-powered search that understands natural language queries and can return semantically relevant results has become a competitive differentiator in breaking news contexts. This approach is comparable to other industry developments, such as the use of machine learning for content recommendation in over-the-top (OTT) platforms. However, the broadcast industry's caution about AI is understandable, given the serious consequences of an AI error in a news context, such as incorrect facial recognition or inaccurate caption content.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the introduction of operational AI has significant implications. Engineers and operations managers must prioritize the deployment sequence and manage the organisational change that comes with it. The organisations that have moved early are accumulating both capability and institutional knowledge at a rate that will make it increasingly difficult for late movers to catch up. To effectively implement operational AI, teams must assess their current workflows and identify areas where automation can deliver the most value. They must also consider the human oversight required to ensure the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated metadata and QC results. By doing so, they can unlock the full potential of operational AI and drive efficiency, productivity, and innovation in their newsrooms.

title: The ST 2110 Transition: Why Small-Market Broadcasters Are Choosing Hybrid-IP Over Full Migration

meta_description: The ST 2110 Transition: Why Small-Market Broadcasters Are Choosing Hybrid-IP Over Full Migration. What Was Announced Full IP migration, the holy grail o...
body_html:
What Was Announced

Full IP migration, the holy grail of broadcast infrastructure modernisation, is proving to be a costly and complex endeavour for small-market broadcasters. As the industry converges on SMPTE ST 2110 as the future of broadcast infrastructure, a hybrid gateway architecture has emerged as a practical alternative for organisations with limited budgets and ageing but functional SDI infrastructure.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The technical case for full IP migration is compelling: uncompressed video over IP, flexible routing, software-defined production, and the ability to run broadcast workflows in the cloud. However, the economics tell a different story for small-market broadcasters, who must consider the cost of replacing or modifying a substantial portion of their signal chain, including cameras, routing switchers, production switchers, multiviewers, monitoring systems, and ingest and playback infrastructure. The hybrid gateway approach offers a more feasible solution, allowing broadcasters to introduce IP connectivity incrementally and selectively, starting with the interconnect between facilities and expanding their IP infrastructure as needed. This approach enables organisations to develop IP engineering competency, deliver measurable operational benefits, and transition to IP-based infrastructure at a pace and scale that their budgets can sustain. The hybrid gateway architecture utilises gateway devices that convert between SDI and IP signals, allowing legacy SDI equipment to participate in an IP workflow without being replaced. This enables broadcasters to introduce IP connectivity incrementally, starting with the interconnect between facilities, and expand their IP infrastructure selectively, replacing SDI equipment with IP-native alternatives as it reaches end of life. The gateway layer handles the conversion at each interface point, adding capability without requiring the existing gear to be replaced. This approach also allows broadcasters to develop IP engineering competency, deliver measurable operational benefits, and transition to IP-based infrastructure at a pace and scale that their budgets can sustain.

Industry Context

The industry is converging on SMPTE ST 2110 as the future of broadcast infrastructure, with major network affiliates, national broadcasters, and large production facilities already embarking on full IP migration programmes. However, for small-market broadcasters, the economics of full migration are challenging, and the complexity of the ST 2110 standard itself is a significant barrier. The hybrid gateway approach is not a new concept, but it has gained traction in recent years as a practical solution for organisations with limited budgets and ageing infrastructure. Comparable approaches, such as cloud-based production infrastructure, are also emerging as an alternative to both full IP migration and hybrid gateway architectures.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the hybrid gateway approach represents a pragmatic middle path that allows organisations to begin the transition to IP-based infrastructure, develop IP engineering competency, and deliver measurable operational benefits without betting the organisation on a high-risk, high-cost full migration programme. Engineers and operations managers should take note of the following: the hybrid gateway approach requires careful system design to manage added latency and complexity; the value of working with vendors and system integrators who have ST 2110 interoperability experience is high; and the risk of relying on vendor claims of compliance without independent verification is real. Moreover, the economics of cloud-based production infrastructure are still challenging, particularly for markets where bandwidth costs are significant, but it is worth evaluating seriously alongside hybrid-IP on-premises approaches.

body_html:
What Was Announced

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) has developed an open technical standard for attaching verifiable digital provenance information to media content, allowing for the verification of the origin and authenticity of footage in the face of increasingly sophisticated AI-generated synthetic media. This standard enables a camera, editing system, or content management platform to cryptographically sign media content with information about its origin, the devices and software involved in its creation, and any modifications made after initial capture. The C2PA standard is being adopted by major camera manufacturers, editing platforms, and media asset management (MAM) systems, with the goal of establishing a chain of trust from the point of original capture to broadcast.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The C2PA standard addresses the challenge of verifying the authenticity of media content in a world where AI-generated synthetic media is becoming increasingly indistinguishable from authentic footage. By establishing a cryptographically secure chain of trust, C2PA enables news organizations to verify the origin and authenticity of footage, reducing the risk of inadvertently broadcasting synthetic content. This is particularly significant in the broadcast news sector, where the reputational cost of broadcasting fabricated content can be severe. The C2PA standard also enables the detection of any modifications made to the content after initial capture, providing an additional layer of verification and trust. Furthermore, the use of cryptographic signing and hashing ensures that any tampering with the content will be detectable, providing a high level of assurance about the authenticity of the footage.

The C2PA standard has significant implications for broadcast workflows, particularly in the areas of ingest, editing, and playout. By integrating C2PA-compliant systems into their workflows, broadcasters can ensure that the media content they broadcast is authentic and has not been tampered with. This requires careful planning and implementation, including the integration of C2PA-compliant cameras, editing systems, and MAM systems, as well as the development of new workflows and procedures for verifying the authenticity of media content. Additionally, the use of C2PA-compliant systems will require broadcasters to have a deep understanding of cryptographic techniques and protocols, such as public key infrastructure (PKI) and digital signatures, in order to ensure the secure and authentic handling of media content.

Industry Context

The development of the C2PA standard is a response to the growing threat of AI-generated synthetic media, which has the potential to undermine trust in the media and create new challenges for broadcast news organizations. The use of cryptographic techniques to verify the authenticity of media content is not new, but the C2PA standard represents a significant step forward in terms of its scope, scale, and industry-wide adoption. The standard is being supported by a range of industry players, including major camera manufacturers, editing platform vendors, and MAM system providers, which will help to drive its adoption and ensure its widespread use. The C2PA standard is also being developed in conjunction with other industry initiatives, such as the SMPTE ST 2110 standard for professional media over managed IP networks, which will help to ensure seamless integration and interoperability with existing broadcast systems and workflows.

The C2PA standard is not the only approach to verifying the authenticity of media content, and other technologies, such as digital watermarking and forensic analysis, are also being developed and deployed. However, the C2PA standard has the potential to become a widely adopted industry standard, due to its openness, scalability, and flexibility. The standard is also being designed to be extensible, allowing it to adapt to new technologies and threats as they emerge, which will help to ensure its long-term relevance and effectiveness. Furthermore, the C2PA standard is being developed in conjunction with other industry initiatives, such as the W3C Verifiable Credentials standard, which will help to ensure that the standard is compatible with a wide range of use cases and applications.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the C2PA standard has significant implications for their workflows, systems, and procedures. Engineers and operations managers will need to ensure that their systems and workflows are compatible with the C2PA standard, and that they have the necessary skills and expertise to implement and manage C2PA-compliant systems. This will require careful planning

title: How Sony Pictures Networks India Delivered Personalized Ad Insertion at Scale on AWS

card_summary: Sony Pictures Networks India has successfully implemented personalized ad insertion at scale using Amazon Web Services (AWS), marking a significant milestone in the company's efforts to enhance its...
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Sony Pictures Networks India just proved you can swap ads in real time for millions of viewers—without a single on-prem server—using AWS cloud tools.

What Happened

Sony Pictures Networks India rolled out personalized ad insertion at scale (think of it like a digital billboard that changes the ad you see based on who you are and what you watch) entirely on Amazon Web Services [Source 1]. The project is live, not a pilot, and replaces older methods that relied on manual steps and fixed hardware [Source 1]. The company says the cloud setup gives them more flexibility, automation, and the ability to handle sudden spikes in ad demand [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

The core of the system is dynamic ad insertion (imagine a video editor who can swap a car ad for a phone ad in the middle of a show, but does it automatically for every viewer) running on AWS infrastructure [Source 1]. While the source doesn’t name specific AWS services (MediaLive, MediaPackage, MediaTailor, etc.), it highlights three technical pillars: 1. Scalability (like a highway that adds lanes automatically when rush hour hits): Cloud resources expand or shrink based on how many ads need to be inserted at once [Source 1]. 2. Metadata management (think of it like the address labels on packages—without them, the ads don’t know where to go): Accurate metadata is called out as critical for matching the right ad to the right viewer [Source 1]. 3. Automation (like a robot that replaces manual cut-and-paste work): The system reduces manual steps compared to traditional ad-insertion workflows [Source 1]. The source doesn’t specify whether the system uses SSAI (server-side ad insertion, where the ad is stitched into the video stream before it reaches your device) or CSAI (client-side ad insertion, where your device swaps the ad after the stream arrives), but it does mention the workflow supports personalized advertising experiences, which typically lean toward SSAI for scalability [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and ops teams, this shifts ad insertion from a hardware-bound bottleneck to a software-defined service. You no longer need to pre-load ad breaks on playout servers or worry about running out of rack space during a major sports event. Instead, you can spin up cloud capacity on demand and pay only for what you use—like switching from buying generators to renting electricity [Source 1]. For ad sales and revenue teams, the system opens the door to addressable advertising (ads targeted to specific households or viewer segments) at scale. The source doesn’t share ROI numbers, but the implication is that better targeting should lift ad yields without increasing headcount [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t name which AWS services (MediaLive, MediaPackage, MediaTailor, etc.) were used in the build.
  • The source doesn’t specify latency figures—how long it takes from ad decision to ad playout on screen.
  • The source doesn’t state whether the system supports live linear channels, VOD, or both.
  • The source doesn’t disclose pricing or cost savings compared to on-prem ad insertion.
  • The source doesn’t mention compliance with ad-tech standards like VAST, VMAP, or SCTE-35.
  • The source doesn’t clarify if the system integrates with existing ad decision servers (ADS) or if it uses a proprietary AWS ad-decision layer.

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Sony Pictures Networks India — How Sony Pictures Networks India Delivered Personalized Ad Insertion at Scale on AWS (2026-03-16)

Scalability (like a highway that adds lanes automatically when rush hour hits): Cloud resources expand or shrink based on how many ads need to be inserted at once [Source 1]. 2. Metadata management (think of it like the address labels on packages—without them, the ads don’t know where to go): Accurate metadata is called out as critical for matching the right ad to the right viewer [Source 1]. 3. Automation (like a robot that replaces manual cut-and-paste work): The system reduces manual steps compared to traditional ad-insertion workflows [Source 1]. The source doesn’t specify whether the system uses SSAI (server-side ad insertion, where the ad is stitched into the video stream before it reaches your device) or CSAI (client-side ad insertion, where your device swaps the ad after the stream arrives), but it does mention the workflow supports personalized advertising experiences, which typically lean toward SSAI for scalability [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and ops teams, this shifts ad insertion from a hardware-bound bottleneck to a software-defined service. You no longer need to pre-load ad breaks on playout servers or worry about running out of rack space during a major sports event. Instead, you can spin up cloud capacity on demand and pay only for what you use—like switching from buying generators to renting electricity [Source 1]. For ad sales and revenue teams, the system opens the door to addressable advertising (ads targeted to specific households or viewer segments) at scale. The source doesn’t share ROI numbers, but the implication is that better targeting should lift ad yields without increasing headcount [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t name which AWS services (MediaLive, MediaPackage, MediaTailor, etc.) were used in the build.
  • The source doesn’t specify latency figures—how long it takes from ad decision to ad playout on screen.
  • The source doesn’t state whether the system supports live linear channels, VOD, or both.
  • The source doesn’t disclose pricing or cost savings compared to on-prem ad insertion.
  • The source doesn’t mention compliance with ad-tech standards like VAST, VMAP, or SCTE-35.
  • The source doesn’t clarify if the system integrates with existing ad decision servers (ADS) or if it uses a proprietary AWS ad-decision layer.

What Was Announced

Telestream has announced a significant advancement in remote production capabilities, dubbed "Remote Production Perfection: From Cloud Capture to Beyond the Edge". This development focuses on streamlining the remote production workflow, allowing teams to capture, process, and distribute content more efficiently. The announcement highlights the ability to automate and scale remote production tasks, reducing operational drag and increasing flexibility for broadcasters.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

This announcement holds significant technical and operational implications for broadcast teams. By enabling cloud-based capture and processing, Telestream's solution addresses a critical pain point in remote production: the need for seamless integration and scalability. The ability to automate and streamline tasks such as ingest, monitoring, and distribution will enable teams to reduce handoffs, improve metadata flow, and accelerate publishing times. Furthermore, this development will allow teams to better predict output under deadline pressure, making it an attractive solution for broadcasters looking to simplify operations while preserving resilience and editorial speed. The underlying technology is likely built upon established standards such as SMPTE ST 2110, which enables the transport of professional media over IP networks. This would allow for the integration of Telestream's solution with existing broadcast infrastructure, reducing the need for costly upgrades or replacements. Additionally, the use of cloud-based processing will enable teams to scale their resources on-demand, reducing the need for expensive hardware investments.

Industry Context

This announcement sits within the broader context of the streaming industry, where buyers and operators are under pressure to increase flexibility without increasing operational drag. Competing technologies, such as those offered by AWS Elemental or Microsoft Azure, are also vying for market share in the remote production space. However, Telestream's solution appears to focus specifically on the needs of broadcast teams, addressing pain points such as scalability, automation, and integration with existing infrastructure. This targeted approach may give Telestream a competitive edge in the market, particularly among broadcasters looking for a more tailored solution. The use of cloud-based processing and automation also aligns with the industry trend towards software-defined infrastructure and the increasing adoption of cloud-based services. This shift is driven by the need for greater flexibility, scalability, and cost-effectiveness in the face of rapidly changing viewer habits and increasing competition in the streaming market.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast teams, this announcement should be treated as a planning signal rather than a hype signal. Engineers and operations managers should review the architecture and map the dependencies before deciding whether to pilot the solution. A controlled test against a live workflow pain point is likely the best next step, rather than a rushed rollout. By evaluating the change against a real-world bottleneck, teams can determine whether the benefits of Telestream's solution outweigh the costs and risks associated with implementation.

title: The Green Broadcast: Can Hybrid Cloud Workflows Actually Reduce a Station's Carbon Footprint?
dek: What Was Announced A recent analysis has revealed that the environmental benefits of cloud production in broadcasting are more complex than initially claimed...
meta_description: The Green Broadcast: Can Hybrid Cloud Workflows Actually Reduce a Station's Carbon Footprint?. What Was Announced A recent analysis has revealed that th...
body_html:
What Was Announced

A recent analysis has revealed that the environmental benefits of cloud production in broadcasting are more complex than initially claimed. While cloud production can offer real carbon savings, these benefits are contingent on specific conditions, including the energy efficiency of the broadcaster's existing infrastructure and the location of the cloud data centers processing their workloads. The study highlights the need for honest accounting and rigorous measurement of carbon emissions in broadcast operations.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The findings of this analysis have significant implications for broadcast engineering and operations teams. The study shows that cloud production can deliver substantial carbon savings, particularly in areas such as travel elimination and outside broadcast vehicle reduction. However, these benefits are largely dependent on the ability to defer hardware replacement through cloud migration, thereby avoiding the energy consumption and material extraction associated with hardware manufacture. To achieve genuine sustainability outcomes, broadcasters must adopt hybrid approaches that combine cloud-based workflows with efficient on-premises infrastructure and remote production techniques. The measurement problem in broadcast sustainability is a major obstacle to honest accounting and effective decision-making. The lack of standardized measurement frameworks and methodologies for attributing cloud energy consumption makes it challenging to compare and verify sustainability claims from vendors and service providers. Broadcasters must develop their own measurement capabilities and adopt frameworks like the Albert sustainability certification scheme to ensure accurate and transparent sustainability reporting.

Industry Context

The broadcast industry's adoption of sustainability as a marketing narrative has created a complex landscape of competing claims and technologies. Cloud production, in particular, has been touted as a carbon-neutral solution, but the reality is more nuanced. Other approaches, such as facility consolidation and efficient on-premises infrastructure, can also deliver significant energy savings. The industry is moving towards a more hybrid and flexible approach, with a focus on combining cloud-based workflows with on-premises infrastructure and remote production techniques. This shift is driven by the need for more accurate and transparent sustainability reporting, as well as the growing regulatory demands for corporate sustainability reporting. The regulatory environment is becoming increasingly demanding, with European sustainability reporting requirements expanding in scope and applying to a wider range of organizations. Broadcasters operating in regulated markets must develop genuine measurement capability and honest accounting practices to ensure compliance with these requirements. The industry is also seeing the adoption of standardized measurement frameworks, such as the Albert sustainability certification scheme, which provides a more rigorous framework for production-level carbon measurement.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

Broadcast engineering and operations teams must take note of the findings of this analysis and develop hybrid approaches that combine cloud-based workflows with efficient on-premises infrastructure and remote production techniques. This requires a deep understanding of the energy consumption and carbon footprint of existing infrastructure and operations, as well as the ability to measure and attribute carbon emissions accurately. Teams must also develop their own measurement capabilities and adopt standardized frameworks to ensure transparent and accurate sustainability reporting. In addition, broadcasters must prioritize the development of their own measurement capabilities and adopt frameworks like the Albert sustainability certification scheme to ensure accurate and transparent sustainability reporting. This will enable them to make informed decisions about technology investments and ensure compliance with regulatory requirements. By adopting a more nuanced and accurate approach to sustainability, broadcasters can achieve genuine environmental benefits and maintain a competitive edge in the industry.

title: Cloud-Native Revolution: Harmonic VOS and Red Hat OpenShift Mastering Video Delivery, Cost, and Scale
dek: Cloud-Native Revolution: Harmonic VOS and Red Hat OpenShift Mastering Video Delivery, Cost, and Scale
meta_description: Cloud-Native Revolution: Harmonic VOS and Red Hat OpenShift Mastering Video Delivery, Cost, and Scale
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Harmonic and Red Hat teamed up to let broadcasters run video workflows like apps on a cloud phone—scaling up or down with demand without the usual IT headache.

What Happened

Harmonic announced a partnership with Red Hat to integrate its VOS (Harmonic’s cloud-native video processing platform) with Red Hat OpenShift (a container application platform that acts like an operating system for cloud apps) [Source 1]. The goal is to simplify how media teams deploy, manage, and scale video delivery workflows by treating them as cloud-native applications [Source 1]. This integration is part of a broader industry shift toward cloud-native and software-defined workflows, where companies like AWS Elemental and Kaltura are also building similar platforms [Source 1]. However, Harmonic and Red Hat’s collaboration stands out by combining video processing with a container platform designed for enterprise-scale orchestration [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

At the core of this announcement is the pairing of two technologies: - **Harmonic VOS**: A cloud-native video processing platform that handles tasks like encoding, transcoding, and packaging for delivery to OTT, social media, and traditional broadcast [Source 1]. (Think of it like a video factory that runs in the cloud instead of on physical hardware.) - **Red Hat OpenShift**: A container application platform that provides the infrastructure to deploy, manage, and scale applications as containers [Source 1]. (Imagine it as a fleet manager for cloud apps, ensuring they run smoothly whether you need one instance or a hundred.) By integrating VOS with OpenShift, media teams can deploy video workflows as cloud-native applications, which means they can scale up or down dynamically to meet demand [Source 1]. This is particularly useful for handling large volumes of content or sudden spikes in viewership, such as during live events or breaking news [Source 1]. The integration also aims to reduce operational complexity by providing a common platform for managing workflows, which can help teams avoid errors and improve efficiency [Source 1]. The source doesn’t specify which video formats, codecs (e.g., HEVC, AV1), or standards (e.g., ST 2110, SCTE-35) are supported by this integration [Source 1]. It also doesn’t detail whether the solution is designed for hybrid (on-prem + cloud) or fully cloud-native environments [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and operations teams, this integration could mean fewer late-night calls to spin up additional encoding capacity during a live event. By treating video workflows as cloud-native applications, teams can scale resources automatically—like adding more lanes to a highway during rush hour—without manually configuring hardware or software [Source 1]. This could reduce operational overhead and free up engineers to focus on quality control or innovation rather than firefighting. For CTOs and budget owners, the promise is cost efficiency. Cloud-native workflows can scale down when demand is low, avoiding the need to over-provision hardware for peak loads [Source 1]. However, the source doesn’t specify pricing models (e.g., pay-as-you-go, subscription) or whether existing Harmonic customers will need to re-architect their workflows to take advantage of this integration [Source 1].

Blind Spots

- The source doesn’t specify which cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, etc.) are supported beyond the mention of Red Hat OpenShift [Source 1]. - There’s no detail on whether this integration supports hybrid (on-prem + cloud) deployments or if it’s cloud-only [Source 1]. - The source doesn’t name any early adopters or pilot customers, leaving questions about real-world performance and reliability [Source 1]. - No mention of specific video formats, codecs, or industry standards (e.g., ST 2110, NMOS, SCTE-35) supported by the integration [Source 1]. - The source doesn’t clarify whether existing Harmonic VOS customers will get this integration as a free upgrade or if it requires a new license or subscription [Source 1].

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Harmonic — Cloud-Native Revolution: Harmonic VOS and Red Hat OpenShift Mastering Video Delivery, Cost, and Scale (2026-03-12)
