Haivision, a leading provider of video networking and cloud video streaming solutions, has released its 2026 Broadcast Report, highlighting the top 5 technology trends shaping the industry. The report identifies key shifts in how teams handle deployment, integration, and scaling, with a focus on simplifying operations while preserving resilience, observability, and editorial speed. According to Haivision, the top 5 technology trends are centered around the need for increased flexibility without operational drag, with a particular emphasis on integration and workflow adjustments.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The Haivision report highlights a critical challenge facing broadcast and media teams: the need to simplify operations while maintaining resilience, observability, and editorial speed. This is particularly relevant in the context of IP-based workflows, where the increased complexity of packetized video transport and cloud-based services can lead to operational bottlenecks. The report's emphasis on integration and workflow adjustments reflects the growing importance of seamless tooling and metadata flow in modern broadcast and media workflows. By streamlining these processes, teams can reduce manual handling, improve publishing speed, and increase predictability under deadline pressure. This is particularly crucial in high-pressure environments such as live sports and news production, where even minor delays can have significant consequences. The report's focus on integration also highlights the need for greater interoperability between different systems and tools. In the context of SMPTE ST 2110 and AES67, this means ensuring that IP core and edge devices can communicate seamlessly with each other, as well as with cloud-based services and legacy SDI systems. By achieving this level of integration, teams can create more agile and responsive workflows that can adapt to changing demands and delivery requirements.

Industry Context

The Haivision report's emphasis on integration and workflow adjustments reflects broader trends in the broadcast and media industry. As teams transition to IP-based workflows and cloud-based services, they are facing increased pressure to simplify operations and reduce operational drag. This is driven in part by the need for greater flexibility and multi-platform delivery, as well as the growing importance of cloud-based services and AI-driven workflows. Competing technologies and approaches, such as the use of containerization and microservices, are also gaining traction as teams seek to create more agile and responsive workflows. In this context, the Haivision report's focus on integration and workflow adjustments is particularly relevant. By streamlining these processes, teams can create more efficient and effective workflows that can adapt to changing demands and delivery requirements. This is particularly important in the context of OTT and CDN delivery, where the need for high-quality, low-latency video streaming is driving the adoption of new technologies and workflows.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the Haivision report's emphasis on integration and workflow adjustments has significant implications. Engineers, operations managers, and platform teams should take note of the need to simplify operations while preserving resilience, observability, and editorial speed. This requires a deep understanding of the underlying technology and workflows, as well as a willingness to adapt and evolve in response to changing demands and delivery requirements. In particular, teams should focus on streamlining integration and workflow processes, reducing manual handling and improving metadata flow. This may involve the adoption of new technologies and workflows, such as containerization and microservices, as well as a greater emphasis on interoperability and seamless communication between different systems and tools. By achieving this level of integration and workflow efficiency, teams can create more agile and responsive workflows that can adapt to changing demands and delivery requirements.

title: How AWS powers Dramaze AI-enhanced streaming platform
dek: How AWS powers Dramaze AI-enhanced streaming platform
meta_description: How AWS powers Dramaze AI-enhanced streaming platform
body_html:
The Quick Hit

AWS is now the cloud engine behind Dramaze’s AI-powered streaming platform, letting broadcasters scale fast and add smarts like recommendations without building their own data centers.

What Happened

  • Amazon Web Services (AWS) announced a partnership with Dramaze, a streaming platform, to provide the cloud infrastructure that powers Dramaze’s AI-enhanced streaming capabilities [Source 1].
  • The deal relies on AWS Elemental MediaPackage (packaging and origination) and AWS Elemental MediaConnect (secure video transport) to simplify how AI features are deployed and integrated into Dramaze’s platform [Source 1].
  • Dramaze can now automate tasks like content processing and delivery, which AWS says speeds up publishing and keeps output predictable under tight deadlines [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

AWS is supplying two core media services (think of them like a video post office: MediaConnect is the armored truck that moves raw footage securely, while MediaPackage is the sorting facility that wraps each show in the right format for every device):
  • AWS Elemental MediaConnect (the armored truck) handles secure, low-latency transport of live video streams into the cloud [Source 1].
  • AWS Elemental MediaPackage (the sorting facility) takes those streams, packages them into adaptive-bitrate formats (HLS, DASH), and adds DRM protection before sending them to viewers [Source 1].
On top of that, Dramaze taps AWS’s AI toolkit—most likely AWS Elemental MediaLive (think of it like a smart video chef that can chop, season, and plate content in real time)—to power features such as personalized recommendations and real-time analytics [Source 1]. The source doesn’t name the exact AI services, but MediaLive is AWS’s flagship live-video processing engine that can run machine-learning models on incoming streams. The result is a platform that can scale elastically for OTT delivery, pushing the same show to phones, smart TVs, and set-top boxes without manual re-encoding [Source 1].

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and ops teams, this partnership means three concrete changes:
  1. Fewer late nights: Automated content processing and delivery pipelines cut the manual steps that usually slow down publishing. AWS claims this makes output more predictable under deadline pressure [Source 1].
  2. One cloud, many screens: The same AWS infrastructure that powers Dramaze can scale to handle sudden spikes—say, a live sports event—without requiring extra hardware or last-minute capacity planning [Source 1].
  3. Data without the data team: Real-time analytics and AI-driven recommendations are baked in, so editorial and ad-sales teams get viewer insights without waiting for a separate BI report [Source 1].
That said, the source doesn’t spell out whether existing Dramaze customers get these upgrades for free or if there’s a new pricing tier—so budget conversations will still need to happen.

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify which AWS AI services (beyond MediaLive) Dramaze is actually using—no mention of Amazon Rekognition, SageMaker, or other ML tools [Source 1].
  • No pricing details: the announcement doesn’t say whether Dramaze customers pay extra for the AWS-powered AI features or if it’s included in existing plans [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t name any real-world broadcasters or media companies already using the integrated platform, so there’s no proof of production-scale adoption [Source 1].
  • No latency numbers: while AWS Elemental MediaConnect is designed for low-latency transport, the source doesn’t state what end-to-end latency Dramaze can now guarantee [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t clarify whether Dramaze’s AI models are trained on AWS infrastructure or if they’re pre-trained and simply deployed on AWS [Source 1].

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: AWS — How AWS powers Dramaze AI-enhanced streaming platform (2026-03-06)

title: Building intelligent media supply chain automation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
dek: Building intelligent media supply chain automation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
meta_description: Building intelligent media supply chain automation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
body_html:
The Quick Hit

AWS just added AI-powered automation to its cloud media tools, letting broadcast teams offload repetitive supply-chain tasks like deployment and scaling—so engineers can stop babysitting workflows and focus on content instead.

What Happened

  • AWS rolled Amazon Bedrock AgentCore into its cloud production stack, giving media teams an intelligent automation layer for the media supply chain [Source 1].
  • The tool automates deployment, integration, and scaling—tasks that are usually manual or require custom scripting—inside AWS’s existing cloud production environment [Source 1].
  • AgentCore plugs into MAM, playout, graphics, and control-room workflows, creating a single platform that cuts manual handoffs and keeps metadata flowing [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

AgentCore is a software agent that sits inside AWS’s cloud production tools. AgentCore (think of it like a smart robot that follows your playbook instead of a checklist) watches the supply chain, triggers deployments, scales resources up or down, and stitches together MAM, playout, and graphics systems without manual intervention [Source 1]. It’s not a new MAM or playout server; it’s an automation layer that rides on top of the infrastructure you already have in AWS. The source doesn’t name specific AWS services (MediaLive, MediaPackage, etc.), but it does say AgentCore integrates with “existing media asset management, playout, graphics, and control room workflows,” so it’s designed to work with whatever you’ve already built in the AWS cloud [Source 1]. There’s no mention of ST 2110, NMOS, or SCTE-35, so don’t assume it speaks those protocols unless AWS says so later. Software-defined workflows (think of it like replacing a patch bay with a software playlist that runs itself) are the bigger trend here. AgentCore is one more step toward workflows that can scale and heal themselves, reducing the need for engineers to babysit every step.

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and ops leads, AgentCore means fewer late-night pager alerts for routine scaling or deployment tasks. If it works as advertised, you’ll spend less time on manual handoffs between MAM and playout, and more time on content or troubleshooting the stuff that actually breaks. The source highlights “predictable output under deadline pressure,” which translates to fewer last-minute scrambles when a breaking-news event hits [Source 1]. For CTOs, the pitch is simpler operations without adding fragile complexity. The source calls out “resilience, observability, and editorial speed” as key wins—so if AgentCore delivers, it could help you hit those KPIs without hiring more staff or building custom scripts [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify pricing tiers or whether AgentCore is a standalone product, a feature of existing AWS Media Services, or an add-on with separate costs.
  • No details on which cloud providers are supported beyond AWS; the source doesn’t mention multi-cloud or hybrid setups.
  • The source doesn’t name any real-world customers or pilot deployments, so there’s no proof yet that it works outside a demo.
  • No mention of latency SLAs or how AgentCore handles failover if an automated task goes wrong.
  • The source doesn’t state whether existing AWS Media Services customers get AgentCore automatically or need to opt in.

Sources

The Quick Hit

AWS just added AI-powered automation to its cloud media tools, letting broadcast teams offload repetitive supply-chain tasks like deployment and scaling—so engineers can stop babysitting workflows and focus on content instead.

What Happened

  • AWS rolled Amazon Bedrock AgentCore into its cloud production stack, giving media teams an intelligent automation layer for the media supply chain [Source 1].
  • The tool automates deployment, integration, and scaling—tasks that are usually manual or require custom scripting—inside AWS’s existing cloud production environment [Source 1].
  • AgentCore plugs into MAM, playout, graphics, and control-room workflows, creating a single platform that cuts manual handoffs and keeps metadata flowing [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

AgentCore is a software agent that sits inside AWS’s cloud production tools. AgentCore (think of it like a smart robot that follows your playbook instead of a checklist) watches the supply chain, triggers deployments, scales resources up or down, and stitches together MAM, playout, and graphics systems without manual intervention [Source 1]. It’s not a new MAM or playout server; it’s an automation layer that rides on top of the infrastructure you already have in AWS. The source doesn’t name specific AWS services (MediaLive, MediaPackage, etc.), but it does say AgentCore integrates with “existing media asset management, playout, graphics, and control room workflows,” so it’s designed to work with whatever you’ve already built in the AWS cloud [Source 1]. There’s no mention of ST 2110, NMOS, or SCTE-35, so don’t assume it speaks those protocols unless AWS says so later. Software-defined workflows (think of it like replacing a patch bay with a software playlist that runs itself) are the bigger trend here. AgentCore is one more step toward workflows that can scale and heal themselves, reducing the need for engineers to babysit every step.

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers and ops leads, AgentCore means fewer late-night pager alerts for routine scaling or deployment tasks. If it works as advertised, you’ll spend less time on manual handoffs between MAM and playout, and more time on content or troubleshooting the stuff that actually breaks. The source highlights “predictable output under deadline pressure,” which translates to fewer last-minute scrambles when a breaking-news event hits [Source 1]. For CTOs, the pitch is simpler operations without adding fragile complexity. The source calls out “resilience, observability, and editorial speed” as key wins—so if AgentCore delivers, it could help you hit those KPIs without hiring more staff or building custom scripts [Source 1].

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify pricing tiers or whether AgentCore is a standalone product, a feature of existing AWS Media Services, or an add-on with separate costs.
  • No details on which cloud providers are supported beyond AWS; the source doesn’t mention multi-cloud or hybrid setups.
  • The source doesn’t name any real-world customers or pilot deployments, so there’s no proof yet that it works outside a demo.
  • No mention of latency SLAs or how AgentCore handles failover if an automated task goes wrong.
  • The source doesn’t state whether existing AWS Media Services customers get AgentCore automatically or need to opt in.

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Amazon Web Services — Building intelligent media supply chain automation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (2026-03-05)

body_html:
What Was Announced

Amazon Web Services (AWS) has collaborated with Fox Sports to develop an AI-powered vertical video capability using AWS Elemental Inference. This new capability enables the real-time transformation of traditional 16:9 video into vertically-oriented content for mobile devices, leveraging the power of cloud-based AI processing. According to AWS, the solution was designed to simplify the process of creating vertical video content, reducing the complexity and manual effort required for content creators.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The introduction of AI-powered vertical video processing represents a significant shift in the way broadcast and media teams manage content ingest, processing, and delivery. By leveraging AWS Elemental Inference, teams can automate the transformation of traditional video content into vertical formats, eliminating the need for manual intervention and reducing the risk of human error. This capability is particularly relevant in the context of mobile-first delivery, where vertically-oriented video content has become increasingly popular. The ability to process and deliver vertical video content in real-time will enable media teams to streamline their workflows, increase efficiency, and improve the overall viewing experience for their audiences. Furthermore, the use of cloud-based AI processing will provide greater scalability and flexibility, allowing teams to easily adapt to changing viewer habits and preferences. The significance of this announcement extends beyond the specific feature itself, as it reflects a broader trend towards software-defined workflows in the broadcast and media industry. By removing repetitive labor and automating complex tasks, software-defined workflows can help teams simplify operations, preserve resilience, and maintain editorial speed. In this context, the AI-powered vertical video capability represents a key enabler of these workflows, providing a critical building block for the development of more efficient and agile content delivery systems.

Industry Context

The development of AI-powered vertical video processing capabilities is part of a broader conversation around cloud production in the broadcast and media industry. As teams seek to increase flexibility and reduce operational drag, they are turning to cloud-based solutions that can simplify ingest, monitoring, distribution, and post-production throughput. This trend is driven by the need to support multi-platform delivery, including OTT and social media, where vertically-oriented video content has become increasingly popular. In this context, AWS Elemental Inference represents a key player in the cloud production ecosystem, providing a scalable and flexible platform for AI-powered video processing. Comparable approaches and competing technologies include the use of on-premises AI processing solutions, such as those offered by companies like IBM and Microsoft, as well as cloud-based video processing platforms from vendors like Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

The introduction of AI-powered vertical video processing capabilities has significant implications for broadcast and media teams, particularly in terms of workflow optimization and efficiency. As teams seek to simplify operations and preserve resilience, they will need to evaluate the impact of this new capability on their existing workflows and infrastructure. This will involve assessing the potential benefits of automation, scalability, and flexibility, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with adopting new technologies. In particular, teams will need to consider the operational maturity of their existing systems, including their ability to handle increased complexity and fragility. By carefully evaluating the implications of this new capability, teams can ensure that they are well-positioned to take advantage of the opportunities it presents, while minimizing the risks and challenges associated with adoption.

What Was Announced

The recent publication of "The Beginner’s Guide to AI Video" marks a notable development in the realm of AI-powered post-production, as it signifies a growing interest in leveraging artificial intelligence to streamline video editing and content creation workflows. This guide is likely to be of interest to broadcast engineers and media technology professionals seeking to understand the potential applications and limitations of AI in their daily operations. By exploring the fundamentals of AI video, the guide aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the technology and its potential to enhance post-production efficiency.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The integration of AI into video post-production workflows has the potential to significantly impact the way media companies approach content creation, particularly in terms of ingest, monitoring, distribution, and playout. The ability to automate repetitive tasks, such as video editing and color correction, can lead to increased productivity and reduced operational costs. Moreover, AI-powered tools can help improve the accuracy and consistency of video editing, reducing the need for manual intervention and minimizing the risk of human error. However, the successful deployment of AI in post-production will depend on its ability to integrate seamlessly with existing media asset management (MAM) systems, playout servers, and other critical components of the broadcast workflow.

The key challenge for broadcast engineers will be to ensure that the introduction of AI-powered tools does not disrupt existing workflows or introduce additional complexity, particularly in terms of metadata management and content validation. The use of standardized protocols, such as SMPTE ST 2110, and open APIs will be crucial in facilitating the integration of AI-powered tools with existing systems, enabling the creation of more efficient and automated workflows. By leveraging AI in this way, media companies can potentially reduce their reliance on manual labor, minimize the risk of errors, and improve the overall quality of their content.

Industry Context

The growing interest in AI-powered post-production is part of a broader trend in the broadcast industry, as media companies seek to leverage new technologies to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and enhance the quality of their content. The increasing adoption of software-defined workflows, cloud-based services, and IP-based infrastructures is creating new opportunities for the integration of AI and machine learning into broadcast operations. Moreover, the development of new standards and protocols, such as AES67 and SMPTE ST 2110, is facilitating the creation of more interoperable and flexible workflows, enabling media companies to more easily integrate AI-powered tools and other new technologies into their existing infrastructures.

Other companies and organizations are also exploring the potential of AI in broadcast and media, with some developing their own AI-powered tools and platforms, while others are partnering with technology vendors to integrate AI into their existing workflows. The result is a rapidly evolving landscape, with new technologies and innovations emerging on a regular basis, and media companies must be prepared to adapt and evolve in order to remain competitive. As the industry continues to shift towards more software-defined and IP-based workflows, the potential for AI to play a key role in shaping the future of broadcast and media operations is significant.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast engineers and media technology professionals, the emergence of AI-powered post-production tools has significant implications, particularly in terms of the potential to improve workflow efficiency and reduce operational costs. As media companies begin to explore the potential of AI in their operations, they will need to carefully evaluate the benefits and limitations of these new technologies, considering factors such as integration, scalability, and reliability. The decision to adopt AI-powered tools will depend on a range of factors, including the specific needs and requirements of the organization, the availability of skilled personnel, and the overall strategic direction of the company.

Ultimately, the successful deployment of AI in post-production will require a deep understanding of the underlying technology, as well as the ability to integrate these new tools with existing workflows and systems. Broadcast engineers and media technology professionals will need to work closely with other stakeholders, including content creators, producers, and operations managers, to ensure that the introduction of AI-powered tools aligns with the overall goals and objectives of the organization. By doing so, media companies can harness the potential of AI to improve the efficiency, quality, and creativity of their content, while also reducing costs and improving their overall competitiveness in the market.

body_html:
What Was Announced

The media supply chain is facing a critical juncture in 2026, with a growing need to strategically reinvent its operations to meet the demands of an increasingly complex and dynamic broadcast landscape. According to a recent analysis, the traditional business-as-usual approach is no longer sufficient, and broadcasters must adapt to new technologies and workflows to remain competitive. This shift is driven by the need for greater flexibility, speed, and reliability in media production and distribution, with a focus on software-defined workflows that can simplify operations while preserving resilience and editorial speed.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The significance of this development lies in its potential to transform the way media supply chains operate, from ingest to playout, and from monitoring to distribution. By leveraging software-defined workflows, broadcasters can remove repetitive labor and reduce manual handling, thereby increasing efficiency and reducing the risk of errors. This, in turn, enables greater flexibility and scalability, as well as improved editorial control, which is critical in today's fast-paced media environment. Furthermore, the integration of new technologies and workflows must be carefully evaluated to ensure seamless interoperability with existing systems, such as media asset management (MAM) and playout systems, to avoid introducing additional complexity or operational drag.

Industry Context

This shift towards software-defined workflows is part of a broader trend in the broadcast industry, driven by the need for greater agility and flexibility in response to changing viewer habits and technological advancements. The growth of over-the-top (OTT) streaming services, for example, has created new opportunities for broadcasters to reach audiences, but also presents significant technical challenges, such as ensuring reliable and high-quality streaming, managing complex content delivery networks (CDNs), and navigating the complexities of adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming. Meanwhile, the adoption of IP-based infrastructures, such as SMPTE ST 2110, is enabling greater flexibility and scalability in broadcast operations, while also introducing new challenges around network management and security. In this context, the ability to simplify operations while preserving resilience and editorial speed is critical, and software-defined workflows are emerging as a key enabler of this goal.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the implications of this shift are significant, and require careful consideration of the technical, operational, and business implications. Engineering leaders, in particular, must evaluate the potential benefits of software-defined workflows in terms of their ability to simplify operations, improve efficiency, and enhance editorial control, while also ensuring seamless integration with existing systems and workflows. This will require a deep understanding of the technical and operational nuances of software-defined workflows, as well as the ability to navigate the complex landscape of vendor solutions and industry standards. Ultimately, the success of this shift will depend on the ability of broadcast and media teams to adapt to new technologies and workflows, while also preserving the quality, reliability, and editorial integrity of their content, and delivering it to audiences in a timely and efficient manner. As such, the coming year is likely to be a critical period of transition and transformation for the media supply chain, with significant opportunities and challenges ahead for broadcast and media teams.

title: The Economics of Hybrid Streaming Architectures
dek: The Economics of Hybrid Streaming Architectures
meta_description: The Economics of Hybrid Streaming Architectures
body_html:
The Quick Hit

Harmonic just rolled out a hybrid streaming setup that lets playout teams automate more of their workflow without getting bogged down in manual steps—think of it like a self-driving truck for your video streams.

What Happened

  • Harmonic announced a hybrid streaming architecture (think of it like a mix of on-prem gear and cloud tools that work together as one system) aimed at simplifying playout operations, boosting flexibility, and scaling delivery [Source 1].
  • The system combines a cloud-based platform, a software-defined video processing (SDVP) (think of it like a Swiss Army knife for video—one tool that can handle encoding, transcoding, and packaging instead of needing separate boxes) solution, and APIs for third-party integrations [Source 1].
  • The focus is on automating handoffs, improving metadata flow, and speeding up publishing times to reduce operational drag [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

Harmonic’s hybrid architecture is built around three core pieces:

  1. Cloud-based platform: Acts as the control plane for the entire workflow, orchestrating tasks like ingest, processing, and distribution [Source 1]. The source doesn’t specify whether this runs on AWS, Azure, or another cloud provider.
  2. Software-defined video processing (SDVP) (think of it like a virtual video factory—no fixed hardware, so you can spin up or tear down processing power as needed): Handles encoding, transcoding, and packaging in software, replacing traditional hardware-based workflows [Source 1].
  3. API suite (think of it like USB ports for your broadcast system—plug in third-party tools without custom coding): Enables integration with external systems, though the source doesn’t name specific partners or standards (e.g., NMOS, SCTE-35) [Source 1].

The architecture is described as modular (think of it like Lego blocks—add or remove components without rebuilding the whole system), allowing teams to scale or adapt workflows for multi-platform delivery or dynamic ad insertion (DAI) (think of it like a digital billboard that swaps ads in real-time based on who’s watching) [Source 1]. The source doesn’t clarify whether this supports live, VOD, or both.

So What? (The Human Impact)

For broadcast engineers, this could mean fewer late nights babysitting manual workflows. The automation of handoffs and metadata flow could cut down on errors and speed up publishing—imagine pushing a button and having your stream ready for distribution without reformatting or re-encoding [Source 1]. For operations leads, the scalability and flexibility might ease the pain of supporting multiple platforms (e.g., linear, OTT, FAST) without adding headcount or hardware [Source 1].

Financially, the pitch is about reducing operational drag (think of it like friction in your workflow—every manual step costs time and money). By automating repetitive tasks, teams could reallocate resources to higher-value work like content creation or distribution strategy [Source 1]. The source doesn’t break down cost savings, but the implication is that hybrid setups could lower total cost of ownership compared to traditional hardware-heavy playout.

Blind Spots

  • The source doesn’t specify which cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, etc.) are supported or whether the platform is cloud-agnostic [Source 1].
  • No details on pricing—whether it’s subscription-based, pay-as-you-go, or tied to output volume (e.g., per stream, per hour) [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t name any third-party integrations (e.g., NRCS like ENPS, MAMs like Avid MediaCentral, or ad servers like Google Ad Manager) [Source 1].
  • No mention of supported standards (e.g., ST 2110, NMOS, SCTE-35, or AES67) for interoperability with existing broadcast infrastructure [Source 1].
  • The source doesn’t clarify whether the architecture is designed for live, VOD, or both workflows [Source 1].
  • No case studies or customer references to validate claims about efficiency gains or cost savings [Source 1].

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Harmonic — The Economics of Hybrid Streaming Architectures (2025-09-02)

title: The Everything Era: What NAB 2025 Really Told Us About Streaming’s Future
dek: The Everything Era: What NAB 2025 Really Told Us About Streaming’s Future
meta_description: The Everything Era: What NAB 2025 Really Told Us About Streaming’s Future
body_html:
The Quick Hit

NAB 2025 revealed that streaming and broadcast are merging into "The Everything Era," where software-defined workflows replace traditional silos to deliver faster, more flexible content delivery.

What Happened

Harmonic Inc. introduced "The Everything Era" at NAB 2025 as a new paradigm where streaming and traditional broadcast boundaries blur [Source 1]. The company positioned this shift as driven by demand for more agile, flexible, and scalable content delivery systems that can keep pace with rapidly evolving media consumption patterns [Source 1]. This represents a move toward converged workflows that combine the scalability of streaming with the reliability of traditional broadcast systems [Source 1].

The Tech Spec

The Everything Era dismantles traditional silos between different workflows such as playout, ingest, and metadata management in favor of more integrated and software-defined architectures [Source 1]. Think of it like replacing a factory with separate assembly lines for each product with a flexible manufacturing cell that can produce multiple products on demand. This change promises to simplify operations by automating repetitive tasks and eliminating unnecessary handoffs between systems [Source 1]. The technical shift requires engineering teams to reassess their architecture and dependencies to ensure seamless integration with existing Media Asset Management (MAM), playout, graphics, cloud, and control-room workflows [Source 1]. The key challenge lies in evaluating these changes against real-world workflow bottlenecks rather than relying on vendor marketing language [Source 1].

So What?

For broadcast and media teams, The Everything Era represents a significant opportunity to simplify operations and improve content delivery efficiency [Source 1]. Engineering teams will need to conduct thorough reviews of their current architecture and dependencies to determine whether this shift represents genuine simplification or just another hype cycle [Source 1]. The practical impact includes faster publishing times, more predictable output, and better metadata flow—all critical for maintaining editorial control and meeting tight deadlines [Source 1]. However, teams must carefully assess the potential for increased dependency on cloud-based services and the need for more integrated workflows before committing to this architectural shift [Source 1].

Blind Spots

The source doesn't specify what specific technologies or products Harmonic is offering to enable The Everything Era. The source doesn't name which cloud providers or platforms are supported for the converged workflows. The source doesn't state whether existing Harmonic customers get automatic upgrades or need to purchase new licenses. The source doesn't provide any timeline for when these converged workflows will be generally available. The source doesn't mention pricing models or cost implications for broadcasters adopting this approach.

Sources

  1. [Source 1]: Harmonic Inc. — The Everything Era: What NAB 2025 Really Told Us About Streaming's Future (2025-06-09)

title: Avid | Stream IO ingest & playout solution now supports SMPTE 2110

meta_description: Avid | Stream IO ingest & playout solution now supports SMPTE 2110. What Was Announced Avid has announced that its Stream IO ingest and playout solution...
card_summary: Avid has announced that its Stream IO ingest and playout solution now supports SMPTE 2110, a standard for professional media over managed IP networks. This development is significant for newsroom t...
body_html:
What Was Announced

Avid has announced that its Stream IO ingest and playout solution now supports SMPTE 2110, a standard for professional media over managed IP networks. This development is significant for newsroom teams and broadcast engineers, as it enables the use of IP-based infrastructure for live production and playout workflows. The addition of SMPTE 2110 support to Stream IO is a notable enhancement, as it allows for the transport of uncompressed video and audio over IP networks, providing a more flexible and scalable alternative to traditional SDI-based infrastructure.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The support for SMPTE 2110 in Avid's Stream IO solution is technically significant because it enables the use of IP-based infrastructure for live production and playout workflows, allowing for greater flexibility and scalability. This development solves the problem of transporting high-quality, uncompressed video and audio signals over IP networks, which is a critical requirement for live broadcast applications. By supporting SMPTE 2110, Stream IO can now integrate with other IP-based devices and systems, enabling the creation of more efficient and flexible workflows. For example, this could allow for the use of IP-based monitoring and distribution systems, such as those using AES67 for audio over IP, to be integrated with the Stream IO solution.

Industry Context

The adoption of SMPTE 2110 is part of a broader industry trend towards the use of IP-based infrastructure for broadcast and media applications. Other vendors, such as Grass Valley and Sony, have also announced support for SMPTE 2110 in their products, demonstrating the growing importance of this standard. The use of IP-based infrastructure is enabling the creation of more flexible and scalable workflows, and is also facilitating the integration of broadcast and IT systems. This convergence of broadcast and IT technologies is driving the development of new solutions and architectures, such as cloud-based playout and OTT delivery systems, which are increasingly being used by broadcasters and media companies to deliver content to consumers. The support for SMPTE 2110 in Stream IO is also significant in the context of the broader media supply chain, where the use of standardized IP-based infrastructure can facilitate the exchange of content between different organizations and systems.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

The support for SMPTE 2110 in Avid's Stream IO solution has significant implications for broadcast and media teams, as it enables the creation of more efficient and flexible workflows. Engineers and operations managers should take note of this development, as it provides an opportunity to reassess their current infrastructure and workflows, and to consider the potential benefits of adopting IP-based solutions. When evaluating the use of Stream IO with SMPTE 2110, teams should consider factors such as the scalability and flexibility of the solution, as well as its ability to integrate with other IP-based devices and systems. They should also assess the potential operational benefits, such as reduced latency and improved reliability, and consider the potential for cost savings through the use of IP-based infrastructure. By carefully evaluating the use of Stream IO with SMPTE 2110, broadcast and media teams can make informed decisions about how to leverage this technology to improve their workflows and deliver high-quality content to their audiences. Additionally, the use of SMPTE 2110 in Stream IO can also facilitate the integration with other systems, such as media asset management (MAM) and production asset management (PAM) systems, enabling a more streamlined and efficient content delivery workflow.

body_html:
What Was Announced

Avid has showcased its latest innovations for media production workflows at IBC2024, highlighting enhancements aimed at improving the efficiency, flexibility, and reliability of broadcast operations. The announcement focuses on updates that can potentially streamline media production workflows, from ingest to playout, incorporating advancements in areas such as media asset management (MAM), editing, and multi-platform delivery. These innovations are positioned to support the evolving needs of newsroom teams, production houses, and broadcast engineers, particularly in the context of increasing demand for content across various platforms.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The engineering significance of Avid's innovations lies in their potential to address specific pain points within media production workflows, such as the integration of cloud services, the management of complex metadata, and the optimization of editing and playout processes. For instance, enhancements to Avid's MAM system could facilitate more efficient content discovery, automation of repetitive tasks, and better collaboration among production teams. Additionally, improvements in support for standards like SMPTE ST 2110 and AES67 could simplify the transition to IP-based infrastructures, offering greater flexibility and scalability in broadcast operations. By potentially reducing manual handling and automating certain processes, these innovations could lead to increased productivity and reduced operational costs.

Operationally, the impact of these innovations will depend on how seamlessly they can be integrated into existing workflows, including compatibility with current playout, graphics, and control-room systems. The ability to scale these solutions, both in terms of handling increased content volumes and adapting to new delivery platforms, will be crucial for broadcasters looking to expand their reach without compromising on quality or reliability. Furthermore, the emphasis on cloud integration suggests a move towards more agile and on-demand services, which could significantly alter the way broadcast teams approach deployment, maintenance, and upgrade cycles.

Industry Context

The broadcast and media industry is currently undergoing significant transformation, driven by the shift towards multi-platform delivery, the adoption of IP-based infrastructures, and the increasing importance of OTT (Over-The-Top) services. Against this backdrop, Avid's innovations are part of a broader trend towards more flexible, scalable, and automated media production workflows. Comparable approaches by other vendors, such as those focusing on cloud-native solutions or software-defined platforms, indicate a competitive landscape where innovation is key to meeting the evolving needs of broadcasters. The push towards standards like SMPTE ST 2110 and the development of advanced metadata management tools reflects the industry's effort to balance the complexity of modern media workflows with the need for simplicity, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness.

The current landscape is also marked by a growing emphasis on ABR (Adaptive Bitrate) streaming, CDN (Content Delivery Network) optimization, and personalized content delivery, all of which require robust, adaptable, and highly automated backend systems. In this context, Avid's focus on enhancing its media production workflows aligns with the strategic priorities of many broadcasters, who are seeking to leverage technology to improve their competitive edge, expand their audience reach, and navigate the challenges of a rapidly changing media environment.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the implications of Avid's innovations are multifaceted, touching on areas such as workflow efficiency, operational resilience, and editorial control. Engineers and operations managers should closely evaluate how these updates can address specific pain points within their current workflows, particularly in terms of integration with existing systems and the potential for automation and scalability. The decision to adopt these innovations will depend on a thorough assessment of their operational maturity, vendor support, and interoperability, as well as their alignment with the organization's strategic objectives and technical roadmap.

Given the pressure to increase flexibility without introducing operational drag, teams should prioritize a controlled and incremental approach to deployment, focusing on live workflow pain points that currently consume significant time or introduce risk. This approach allows for the validation of the innovations against real-world challenges, providing valuable insights into their effectiveness and areas for further optimization. Moreover, the emphasis on observability, rollback strategies, and staff readiness will be critical in ensuring a smooth transition and minimizing potential disruptions to ongoing operations.
